title: Museum Maps
section: Number of museums in each state
text:
Number of museums in each state

Interactive map with leaflet


Code
# set up -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# setting bins and customizing color scale
bins = c(0, 20, 40, 80, 120, 160, 200, 260, 320, 400, 600, 800)
pal <- colorBin(viridis(12), domain = museum_sf$total, bins = bins)
#viridis(12) uses the viridis scale when making color bins

# creating the labels
museum_sf <- museum_sf |>
  mutate(labels = str_c(State, ": ", total, " museums in total"))
# produces strings like "Idaho: x museums in total"

# making the labels html
labels <- lapply(museum_sf$labels, HTML)

# creates a floating legend of the data source - used
#https://r-graph-gallery.com/package/leaflet.html
# for help writing the original css code, then customised
legend <- "
<style>
  .custom-legend {
    background-color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);
    padding: 5px;
    border-radius: 5px;
    border: 1px solid #ddd;
    transition: background-color 0.3s, transform 0.3s;
    width: 300px;
  }
  .custom-legend:hover {
    background-color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.9);
    transform: scale(1.05);
  }
</style>
<div>
 <p>
     Data source: Institute of Museum and Library Services, <a href = https://www.imls.gov/research-evaluation/data/museum-data-files>https://www.imls.gov/research-evaluation/data/museum-data-files</a>
  </p>
</div>"

# changes the dataframe class to sf so it can be used in leaflet
museum_sf <- st_as_sf(museum_sf)

# making the map ---------------------------------------------------------------
leaflet(museum_sf) |>
  setView(-96, 37.8, 4) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(total), # fill thte state outlines with the palette
    weight = 2, # border line weight
    opacity = 1, # border fully opaque
    color = "white", # white borders
    dashArray = "3", # dashed borders
    fillOpacity = 0.7, # makes the state fills slightly transparent
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions( # options for mouse hovering
      weight = 5, #heavier border
      color = "white", # border color
      dashArray = "", #undashed lines
      fillOpacity = 0.7, #fill opacity stays the same
      bringToFront = TRUE),
    label = labels, # puts the labels on the map
    labelOptions = labelOptions(
      style = list("font-weight" = "normal", 
                   padding = "3px 8px", # put a border around the text
                   color = "black"), # text color
      textsize = "15px",
      direction = "auto")) |>
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~total, opacity = 0.7, title = NULL, 
    position = "bottomright") |> # puts a color legend on the map
  addControl(html = legend, # adds the custom css legend/caption
             position = "bottomleft", 
             className = "custom-legend")








Static map with ggplot


Code
museum_polygon |>
   ggplot(mapping = aes(x = long, y = lat, # maps the state shapes
                          group = group)) + 
  geom_polygon(aes(fill = total), color = "white", # white borders, fill scale
               linewidth = 0.1) + 
  labs(fill = "Number of Museums",
       title = "Number of Museums in Each US State",
       subtitle = "Excluding Alaska and Hawaii",
       caption = "Data source: Institute of Museum and Library Services, https://www.imls.gov/research-evaluation/data/museum-data-files") +
  coord_map() + 
  theme_void() + #white background
  scale_fill_viridis(trans = "log", breaks = c(50 ,150, 400)) 









Code
# rescales the fill scale so that smaller
# values have more space in between them than larger ones


The three states with the most museums are New York, Texas, and California, with astronomically larger numbers than every other contiguous US state. The three states with the fewest museums are North Dakota, Maryland, and Vermont. Looking at the entire gradient of the map, it seems like East Coast states have more museums, and the numbers generally decreases as you move West.
It’s interesting to see that there is some similarity between population and museum count, since California and Texas–two states with the largest populations–also have the most museums. This is also the case for size – two very small states, Maryland and Rhode Island, both have a smaller amount of museums. However, this isn’t true across the board, since large Western states like Nevada have under 50, and many of the smaller Eastern states also have larger numbers.

title: Museum Maps
Museum Maps
text:
Individual Museums and Types
This map colors the states by the most common type of museum, of six: Art Museum, Arboretum, Botanical Garden, or Nature Center, Children’s Museum, History Museum, Natural History or Natural Science Museum, Science & Technology Museum or Planetarium, and Zoo, Aquarium, or Wildlife Conservation Organization. Each point is a specific museums’s location, with the museum type. You can zoom in and hover over the points to find out about them!


Code
leaflet(disci_sf) |>
  setView(-96, 37.8, 4) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(most_common),
    weight = 2,
    opacity = 1,
    color = "white",
    dashArray = "3",
    fillOpacity = 0.7) |>
  addCircles(lng = ~LONGITUDE, 
             lat = ~LATITUDE, 
             radius = 1, 
             color = "#440154",
             fillColor = "#440154",
             fillOpacity = 0.7,
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(
      color = "white",
      fillColor = "white",
      bringToFront = TRUE),
    label = labels,
    labelOptions = labelOptions(
      style = list("font-weight" = "normal", padding = "3px 8px", color = "black"),
      textsize = "15px",
      direction = "auto")) |>
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~most_common, opacity = 0.7, title = "Most Common Museum Type", labels = c("Art", "History"),
    position = "bottomright") |>
  addControl(html = legend, position = "bottomleft", className = "custom-legend")
